module.title: 3 · Interpreting coefficients: odds ratios & marginal effects
module.summary: A raw logit coefficient is a change in log-odds — not very intuitive. Exponentiate it to get an odds ratio (a multiplicative effect on the odds), or compute a marginal effect dP/dx (the change in probability), which is largest near p=0.5 and shrinks at the extremes.

stages.title: Three currencies for the same effect
stages.html:
Log-odds, odds, or probability?

The estimated β₁ is in log-odds units, which almost nobody thinks in. We translate it into two friendlier currencies.

Odds ratio: e^(β₁)

Because the log-odds are linear, exponentiating undoes the log:

odds-ratio = e^(β₁)

A one-unit rise in x₁ multiplies the odds by e^(β₁). If β₁ = 0.7 then e^(0.7) ≈ 2.0: the odds double. If e^(β₁) > 1 the feature raises the odds; if < 1 it lowers them; if = 1 it has no effect. This factor is constant everywhere — that is the elegance of the odds scale.

Marginal effect: dP/dx

People often want the effect on the probability, not the odds. For logit:

∂P/∂x₁ = β₁ · p · (1 − p)

This is not constant — it depends on where you are on the curve. It peaks at p = 0.5 (factor 0.25·β₁) and vanishes as p → 0 or 1. statsmodels averages it across the sample with res.get_margeff() (the Average Marginal Effect).

Key idea. Odds ratio = constant multiplicative effect on the odds. Marginal effect = change in probability, biggest in the middle of the S, smallest at the tails.

stages.title: Reading the numbers correctly
stages.html:
Pitfalls to avoid

  • Do not read the raw β as a probability change — it is a log-odds change.
  • An odds ratio of 2.0 does not mean the probability doubles. Going from 50% (odds 1) to odds 2 is 67%, not 100%.
  • The marginal effect needs a reference point. Average Marginal Effect (AME) computes dP/dx for every observation and averages — usually the most honest summary. Marginal Effect at the Means (MEM) plugs in the average x instead.
  • For a binary regressor, the cleaner summary is the discrete change in predicted probability from 0 to 1, not the derivative.

Rule of thumb for logit: divide a coefficient by 4 to get the maximum marginal effect on probability. β₁ = 1.5 → up to about 0.375 change in probability per unit of x, near p = 0.5.

Key idea. The 'divide-by-4' rule gives the steepest possible probability effect; the actual average marginal effect is usually smaller because most observations sit off the p=0.5 peak.

stages.title: Odds ratios and average marginal effects
stages.note: We fit logit, exponentiate the coefficients to read odds ratios, and call get_margeff() for the average marginal effects (the change in probability). Notice the AME for x1 is well below β1/4 — most observations are off the steepest part of the curve.
stages.code:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 800
x1 = rng.normal(0, 1, n); x2 = rng.normal(0, 1, n)
eta = -0.3 + 1.5*x1 - 0.8*x2
p = 1/(1+np.exp(-eta)); y = rng.binomial(1, p)
df = pd.DataFrame({'y': y, 'x1': x1, 'x2': x2})

res = smf.logit('y ~ x1 + x2', df).fit(disp=0)
odds = np.exp(res.params)
print('Coefficients (log-odds):')
print(np.round(res.params, 3).to_string())
print('\nOdds ratios  exp(coef):')
print(np.round(odds, 3).to_string())
print('\nInterpretation: +1 in x1 multiplies the odds by %.2f' % odds['x1'])
print('               +1 in x2 multiplies the odds by %.2f (i.e. lowers them)' % odds['x2'])
print('\ndivide-by-4 max marginal effect for x1: %.3f' % (res.params['x1']/4))
print('\n', res.get_margeff().summary())

stages.title: See the marginal effect change along the curve
stages.note: Pick a slope β₁ and a point x*. The orange dot is P(y=1) there; the dashed tangent is the local slope dP/dx = β₁·p·(1−p). Drag x* toward the tails and watch the tangent flatten even though β₁ never changes — that is why 'the' marginal effect is not a single number.
stages.template:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
b1 = {{b1}}; b0 = 0.0; xstar = {{xstar}}
xs = np.linspace(-6, 6, 300)
P = 1/(1+np.exp(-(b0+b1*xs)))
ps = 1/(1+np.exp(-(b0+b1*xstar)))
slope = b1*ps*(1-ps)            # dP/dx at x*
tang = ps + slope*(xs - xstar)
plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
plt.plot(xs, P, color='#da9100', lw=2.4)
plt.plot(xs, np.clip(tang,-0.1,1.1), color='#6f6b57', lw=1.5, ls='--')
plt.scatter([xstar],[ps], color='#af983f', zorder=5, s=40)
plt.ylim(-0.03,1.03); plt.xlabel('x'); plt.ylabel('P(y=1)')
plt.title('at x*=%.1f:  P=%.3f   dP/dx=%.3f   (max=%.3f)' % (xstar, ps, slope, b1/4))

stages.title: Check
stages.prompt: A logit gives a coefficient of 0.69 on x₁. What is the cleanest one-line interpretation?
choices: A one-unit rise in x₁ raises P(y=1) by 0.69
A one-unit rise in x₁ roughly doubles the odds of y=1, since e^0.69≈2
A one-unit rise in x₁ doubles the probability of y=1
x₁ explains 69% of the variation in y
stages.explain: e^0.69 ≈ 2, so the odds (not the probability) are multiplied by about 2 — the odds ratio is the constant, exponentiated read of a logit coefficient.

stages.title: Check
stages.prompt: Why is the average marginal effect (dP/dx) usually smaller than coefficient/4?
choices: Because statsmodels uses robust standard errors
Because coefficient/4 is the maximum effect, reached only at p=0.5, and most observations sit away from there
Because marginal effects ignore the intercept
Because the AME is measured in odds, not probability
stages.hint: Where on the S-curve is p·(1−p) largest?
stages.explain: The factor p·(1−p) peaks at 0.25 when p=0.5, giving the divide-by-4 maximum; observations in the flatter tails contribute smaller slopes, pulling the average below that peak.

stages.title: Turn the coefficient into an odds ratio
stages.prompt: A logit gives a coefficient of 0.69 on treated. The odds ratio is exp(β). Enter exp(0.69) to two decimals (a plain number, no units).
stages.hint: exp(0.69) is just under 2. This multiplies the ODDS — it is not a change in probability.
stages.explain: exp(0.69) = 1.99 ≈ 2.00 — treatment roughly DOUBLES the odds. This is the odds-ratio reading of a logit coefficient, and it is constant across x. It is NOT a doubling of the probability and NOT the marginal effect on P(y=1): odds and probability move together only when p is small. Boundary: the odds ratio e^β is the one effect measure that does stay constant; the probability effect β·p(1−p) does not.

stages.title: The marginal effect at p = 0.5
stages.prompt: A logit gives β=0.8 on a binary treatment. At a baseline probability p=0.5, the marginal effect on P(y=1) is β·p(1−p). Enter it to two decimals (a probability change, e.g. 0.20).
stages.hint: Plug in: 0.8 × 0.5 × (1−0.5). The answer is a quarter of β here, not β itself.
stages.explain: This is the coefficient-is-a-marginal-effect trap in numbers: the marginal effect is β·p(1−p) = 0.8·0.25 = 0.20, NOT the coefficient 0.8. And it shrinks toward the tails — at p=0.9 it is only 0.8·0.09 = 0.072. That p-dependence is exactly why you cannot read a logit coefficient as a single, constant change in probability. Boundary: p(1−p) peaks at 0.25 (p=0.5), so β/4 is the largest the marginal effect can ever be; everywhere else it is smaller.

stages.title: Reading a logit coefficient — select all
stages.prompt: A logit reports β=0.69 on treated. Select all that apply — which statements are correct readings of this coefficient?
choices: It adds 0.69 to the log-odds of y=1 for a one-unit change in treated
The odds of y=1 are multiplied by about 2 (e^0.69 ≈ 2)
It raises the probability P(y=1) by 0.69
It is the marginal effect dP/dx, the same at every value of x
The effect on probability depends on the baseline p, peaking near p=0.5
stages.hint: Two correct statements live on the log-odds/odds scale; one more is about how the probability effect varies. The two probability-as-constant statements are the trap.
stages.explain: Correct readings: β adds to the log-odds (0), the odds are multiplied by e^β ≈ 2 (1), and the probability effect varies with the baseline p, peaking near p=0.5 (4). The two distractors are the coefficient-is-a-marginal-effect trap: β is NOT a 0.69 jump in probability (2) and NOT a constant dP/dx (3) — the probability effect is β·p(1−p), which changes along the S-curve. Boundary: only the log-odds increment and the odds ratio e^β are constant; any probability statement must name the p at which it is evaluated.
